html:
The big picture

This lecture is about using a robot rather than building one. A robot is commanded either joint by joint (forward operation, i.e. forward kinematics) or by a target in x/y/z (inverse operation, i.e. inverse kinematics), as target positions, velocities, a trajectory of waypoints, or forces/torques. Who produces those commands defines the four ways to operate a robot, in increasing autonomy: manual operation (a human steers live), teaching (a human guides once, the robot records and replays), programming (code, often a state machine that reacts to sensors) and autonomous operation. Every mode needs boundary limits on each joint, a work envelope, and must keep clear of singularities. The robot's parts and computers talk over communication systems that trade reliability against speed (TCP vs UDP) or guarantee timing (deterministic fieldbuses such as ControlNet/DeviceNet and EtherCAT); ROS is the common robotics middleware, in which nodes exchange messages over topics (and on-demand services). Robots are programmed in anything from blocks (Scratch/Blockly) and G-code to Python and C/C++, and developed and tested first in simulation (CoppeliaSim, game engines, Gazebo), up to a digital twin of the real machine. When commands come from several sources at once, a fixed priority order decides (high-level vs low-level control): hard-wired safety first, then direct manual control, then remote or automated control.

Basics of robot operation

  • Forward operation: setting joint angles directly (forward kinematics).
  • Inverse operation: setting a target in x/y/z (inverse kinematics). More details later…

  • What can be commanded:

    • Target position ([x, y, z] or angle)
    • Velocity (per joint or in [x, y, z])
    • (Acceleration)
    • Trajectory: multiple waypoints (path)
    • Force / torque (depending on the type of joint)
Intuition

The same pose can be described in two "languages". Joint space: "joint 1 to 30°, joint 2 to −45°, …" maps one-to-one onto motor commands, so the robot can execute it directly, but it is hard for a human to tell where the gripper ends up. Cartesian space: "gripper to x = 0.4\ \text{m}, y = 0.1\ \text{m}, z = 0.2\ \text{m}" is what a task is usually stated in, but the controller must first solve for the joint angles (inverse kinematics), which may have several solutions or none. A trajectory is a sequence of such targets (waypoints) that the robot passes through in order. The last bullet differs in kind: force/torque commands say how hard to push, not where to go. Revolute joints take a torque, prismatic joints a force (joint types: 1 Introduction).

Connection

"More details later" refers to the kinematics lecture. In the vault the maths for both directions is already in 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics (25W numbering), including the reachability check for a two-link arm used in 5 AI for Engineers.

How to operate a robot?

  • Manual operation (including tele-operation)
  • Teaching
  • Programming
  • Autonomous (with or without AI)

Pictured: a teach pendant, the hand-held control panel of an industrial robot, with an emergency-stop button.

Intuition

The four modes differ in who decides each motion, and when. Manual: a human decides now, continuously. Teaching: a human decides once, in advance, and the robot repeats it. Programming: an engineer decides in advance, in code, including how to react to sensor events. Autonomous: the robot decides at run time from its own perception and goals, using planning algorithms or learned (AI) models. There is no slide on autonomous operation in this lecture; 5 AI for Engineers (agents: choose a step, observe, choose the next one) shows the same decide–act–observe loop.

Manual operation

  • A user operates the robot with the control panel, a joystick or any other RC.
  • Direct control via API.
  • The robot should stop if no further input commands are given.
  • Commonly used for complex tasks with high variation of the environment.

  • Examples:

    • Cranes (forest, shipyards, …)
    • Humanoid robots with bodysuit control
    • Exploration robots (deep sea, caves)

The slide also shows a browser-based joint-control interface with one panel per joint (e.g. "J2_shoulder") and sliders for position, velocity and effort.

Why should a manually operated robot stop when the input stops?

Because "no input" is ambiguous: the operator may have let go on purpose, or the cable, radio link or operator's PC may have failed. If the robot kept executing its last command (say, "rotate joint 1 at 30°/s"), a lost connection would turn into an uncontrolled motion. So the safe default is a dead-man behaviour: a command is valid only while it keeps being renewed (a held button, a stream of joystick packets), and the robot stops when it stops arriving. Losing the link then produces a stop, not a collision.

Teaching

  • Teaching is the process of manually guiding a robot — either by hand or with the control panel, joystick, RC, …
  • The robot stores the trajectory as waypoints, either manually or at certain intervals.
  • The robot is then able to "replay" the taught trajectory.
  • Commonly used in industrial applications with fixed paths.
  • E.g. welding robots.
Common mistake

"Teaching and manual operation are the same thing: a human moves the robot." The difference is what happens afterwards. In manual operation the robot follows the human live and stops when the input stops; nothing is stored. In teaching the human's motion is recorded as waypoints, and later the robot repeats it on its own, as often as needed, without the human. That is why teaching suits fixed-path jobs like welding, and manual operation suits jobs where every situation is different (cranes, exploration).

Programmed trajectories

  • The robot replays trajectories that are coded in a supported programming language.
  • The robot can be programmed as a state machine to perform a set of changing pre-defined tasks.
  • Sensor readings can be used to alter the robot path (obstacle avoidance).

A state machine: from State 1, event X leads to State 2 and event Y leads to State 3. (Source: MDN Web Docs.)

Intuition

A state machine (finite-state machine) is a program made of a fixed set of states, of which exactly one is active at any time, and transitions between them, each triggered by an event (a sensor reading, a finished motion, a timer). In each state the robot does one well-defined thing; it changes state only when one of that state's events happens. This makes behaviour easy to read and test: every possible path is a path through the diagram.

Worked example — a sorting cell as a state machine

Task: a robot takes parts from a conveyor and puts good parts in bin A and faulty ones in bin B.

  1. List the states (what the robot is doing): IDLE (waiting at home pose), GRASP (move to part, close gripper), INSPECT (hold part in front of a camera), PLACE_A, PLACE_B (move to a bin, open gripper).
  2. List the events (what makes it change): part_detected (light barrier), grip_ok / grip_failed (gripper sensor), part_good / part_bad (camera result), released (gripper open).
  3. Draw the transitions: IDLE → GRASP on part_detected; GRASP → INSPECT on grip_ok; GRASP → IDLE on grip_failed; INSPECT → PLACE_A on part_good, → PLACE_B on part_bad; PLACE_A/PLACE_B → IDLE on released.
  4. Check completeness: every state has an exit for every event that can occur there. A state without one is where the robot would hang (here: what if the camera gives no result? Add a timeout event INSPECT → PLACE_B).
  5. Add sensor-based path changes: the slide's obstacle avoidance becomes one more event, obstacle_detected, leading from every moving state to a PAUSE state.
stateDiagram-v2
  IDLE --> GRASP: part_detected
  GRASP --> INSPECT: grip_ok
  GRASP --> IDLE: grip_failed
  INSPECT --> PLACE_A: part_good
  INSPECT --> PLACE_B: part_bad / timeout
  PLACE_A --> IDLE: released
  PLACE_B --> IDLE: released

Boundaries & limits

  • Each joint/motor needs boundary limits for position/angle, velocity and torque/force.
  • Work envelope.
  • Prevent damage to the surroundings, humans or the robot itself.
  • Per default, self-harming robot poses are not disabled or can disabled by low-level control on mistake.
  • Singularity.

Pictured: a Niryo arm with one joint circled, the joint whose limits are meant.

Unclear (slide 11)

The bullet "Per default, self harming robot poses are not disabled or can disabled by low-level control on mistake" is garbled (the same wording was in last year's deck). The most likely meaning: by default a robot does not automatically prevent poses in which it collides with itself, and where such protection exists it can be switched off by mistake through low-level control. So self-collision limits have to be configured and checked deliberately.

Intuition

The work envelope (workspace) is the set of all points the robot's tool can reach, given its link lengths and joint limits; anything outside it cannot be reached at all. Limits work at two levels. Joint limits (angle, speed, torque per joint) protect the robot's own mechanics and motors. Workspace limits (forbidden zones, a reduced envelope, a maximum tool speed) protect the surroundings and people. A command that would violate any of them should be rejected or clipped before it reaches the motors.

Worked example — checking a command against joint limits

A joint has the limits: angle -170^\circ to +170^\circ, speed at most 180^\circ/\text{s}. It is at +120^\circ and is commanded to +160^\circ, in 0.1\ \text{s}.

  1. Position check: +160^\circ lies inside [-170^\circ, +170^\circ] ✓.
  2. Speed check (average speed = angle change / time): (160^\circ - 120^\circ)/0.1\ \text{s} = 400^\circ/\text{s} > 180^\circ/\text{s} ✗.
  3. Consequence: the target itself is allowed, but not this fast. The motion must take at least 40^\circ / (180^\circ/\text{s}) \approx 0.22\ \text{s}, so the controller either slows the motion down or rejects the command.
  4. Lesson: a target inside the limits does not make a motion safe; every limit (position, velocity, torque) is checked separately.

Singularity

A six-axis arm (a UR cobot) in a singular pose, with the straight-line tool path it is meant to follow (Source: RoboDK blog, "Robot singularities").

What is a singularity, and why is it dangerous?

A singularity is a pose in which the robot loses a degree of freedom: the tool can no longer move in some direction, because two or more joint axes line up (two wrist axes collinear, or the arm fully stretched out). Close to such a pose, moving the tool slowly along a straight line can require some joints to turn extremely fast, in the limit infinitely fast. The controller then either stops with an error or produces sudden, violent joint motions. Joint-space commands (forward operation) are unaffected; the problem appears when a Cartesian path (inverse operation) passes through or near a singular pose, which is why such paths are planned to avoid them.

Common mistake

"Singularities only happen at the edge of the workspace." The fully stretched arm (elbow singularity) is at the edge, but the wrist singularity (two wrist axes in line) and the shoulder singularity (wrist centre directly above the base axis) lie inside the work envelope, in poses that look harmless. A path can be well within reach and still pass through one.

Communication

  • TCP/IP or UDP
  • ControlNet
  • DeviceNet
  • EtherCAT
  • ROS / ROS 2
  • Many more…

(Picture source: www.mathsisfun.com.)

TCP/IP (Ethernet or wireless) / UDP

  • TCP/IP: Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol.
  • IP ensures that each package knows where to go, but doesn't care if all parts of the data arrive or in what order.
  • TCP checks if all packages are there and in the correct sequence. If a package is missing or out of order, TCP will ask to (re)send or (re)arrange the packages.
  • UDP: User Datagram Protocol — no guarantee for order/arrival, but it is much faster. It is useful when speed is important and the loss of some packages is not crucial.

TCP: slower but more reliable transfers (typical: file transfer, web browsing, email). UDP: faster but not guaranteed ("best effort"; typical: live streaming, online games, VoIP). Source: Spiceworks.

Intuition

("Package" on the slides means packet, one chunk of data sent over the network.) IP is the address on the envelope. TCP is registered mail with numbered envelopes: the receiver confirms what arrived, missing ones are sent again, and the data is handed over complete and in order. That costs a connection set-up, acknowledgements and waiting. UDP is a postcard: sent once, no confirmation, no reordering, and nothing waits for anything.

Why would anyone choose UDP for a robot?

For streams of fresh values, a late packet is worse than a lost one. A joint-state or camera stream at 100 Hz sends a new value every 1/100\ \text{s} = 10\ \text{ms}. If one packet is lost, TCP holds back every later packet until the lost one has been resent, which takes at least one retransmission timeout (often hundreds of ms), and by then the resent value is out of date while the newer ones wait behind it. With UDP the next packet simply arrives 10 ms later and the loss costs one sample. TCP is the right choice where every byte must arrive: uploading a robot program, configuration files, logs.

ControlNet (fieldbus) / DeviceNet

  • Open industrial network protocol for industrial automation applications.
  • Network protocol used in the automation industry to interconnect control devices for data exchange.
  • Built-in support for fully redundant cables (ControlNet).
  • Highly deterministic and strictly scheduled.
Intuition

A fieldbus is an industrial network that connects the controller to the devices "in the field": drives, sensors, valves, I/O modules. Deterministic means the timing is guaranteed: each device's data arrives at a fixed point in a fixed cycle, every cycle, not merely fast on average. A joint controller that needs a new setpoint every millisecond needs it every millisecond; an office network is fast on average but can occasionally delay a packet behind other traffic. Redundant cables (ControlNet) mean that one cut cable does not stop the machine.

EtherCAT (Ethernet for Control Automation Technology)

  • Open, high-performance Ethernet-based fieldbus system, primarily used in industrial automation environments for real-time control applications.
  • Fast & deterministic. Uses Ethernet hardware (LAN cables).
  • In EtherCAT, data frames are processed "on the fly". As the data frame travels through each node (device), each node reads the data addressed to it and can insert new data back into the frame in real time.

The slide's analogy (Source: Grok): EtherCAT is like a high-speed train passing through several stations without stopping. The train is the data frame; each station is a device on the network. As the train passes, each station quickly grabs its own mail (data) and drops off mail (new data) for others; the train never stops, which makes delivery very efficient. This makes EtherCAT ideal where timing, speed and real-time control are of utmost importance, as in automated factories, robotics and other high-precision systems.

Why is "on the fly" processing faster than ordinary Ethernet?

In ordinary Ethernet every device gets its own frames: the controller sends one frame per device, each is received completely, handled, and answered with another frame, so a cycle needs many frames and each device adds its full processing delay. In EtherCAT one frame passes through all devices in a line; each device's hardware reads its bytes and writes its answer while the frame is passing through, delaying it only by a tiny, fixed amount. The frame returns to the controller with every device's input data after one round trip. Few frames, fixed delays: that makes it both fast and deterministic.

ROS (Robot Operating System)

  • Open-source robotics middleware.
  • More like a framework than an actual OS.
  • ROS / ROS 2 (for industrial applications, more security).
  • Allows easy communication between robots, external computers & sensors.

  • Messages (published continuously) & services (published on demand):

    • Standard data types (integer, float, double, string)
    • Special data types for sensors & actuators: GPS, LiDAR, depth camera, joint control
Common mistake

"ROS is an operating system like Windows or Linux." Despite the name, ROS runs on top of an operating system (usually Ubuntu Linux). It is middleware: libraries, tools and conventions that let separate programs pass data to each other in standard formats. You install ROS on Ubuntu, not instead of it.

  • Network with one core/head/master and multiple clients.
  • A core can run on the robot or on any other (remote) processing unit.
  • Clients must be on the same network (cable, wireless).
  • A node is an executable script. Multiple nodes can run on a single unit.
  • Nodes exchange messages as "topics" (booleans, sensor data, motor control).
  • Topics are custom and use standard message types.
  • Custom message types can be created.

A publisher node registers its topic name with the ROS master; a subscriber node subscribes to that topic name and receives information about the publisher from the master; after that, ROS messages flow directly from publisher to subscriber via the topic. (Source: trojrobert.github.io.)

Intuition

A topic is a named channel, like a radio frequency. A node that publishes on it broadcasts messages there without knowing who listens; a node that subscribes receives everything published there without knowing who sends. The master is only the directory that introduces them; the data then flows directly between the nodes. A service is the other pattern: a request–reply call made only when needed ("compute an inverse-kinematics solution for this target"), rather than a continuous stream ("current lidar scan, 10 times per second").

Worked example — wiring a stop-on-obstacle function in ROS

Goal: a mobile robot stops when its lidar sees something closer than 0.5\ \text{m}.

  1. Split the job into nodes, one job each: lidar_driver reads the sensor; safety_monitor decides; motor_controller drives the wheels.
  2. Connect them with topics: lidar_driver publishes scans on /scan (a standard LiDAR message type); safety_monitor subscribes to /scan and publishes True/False on /obstacle (a boolean); motor_controller subscribes to /obstacle and stops while it is True.
  3. Decide where each node runs: the drivers on the robot's computer, the monitor anywhere on the same network; the master introduces them.
  4. See the payoff: replacing the lidar with a different model means writing a new lidar_driver only. As long as it publishes the same message type on /scan, the other two nodes are unchanged.
  5. Know the limit: this is a software stop. It complements, and never replaces, the hard-wired emergency stop (see Order of robot control).
  • ROS is also used for easy communication between computers, or even between different software on the same machine.
  • Actual robotic hardware is not needed.
  • Vast online community / online documentation.
  • Last ROS 1 distro for Ubuntu 20.04 / Win 10 (11) (pictured: Noetic Ninjemys).
  • ROS 2 distro Ubuntu 24/26 / Win 11 (pictured: Iron Irwini).
Unclear (slide 20)

The ROS 2 line and its picture don't match. The pictured ROS 2 distribution, Iron Irwini, targets Ubuntu 22.04 and has already reached end of life. The current long-term-support ROS 2 distributions are Jazzy Jalisco for Ubuntu 24.04 and Lyrical Luth for Ubuntu 26.04. Also, the ROS 1 distribution shown (Noetic, the last ROS 1 release) has itself reached end of life (May 2025), so new projects use ROS 2. Check the current list at docs.ros.org before installing.

ROS – visualization

  • RQT Plot — plotting values (e.g. sensor signals) over time.
  • RViz — 3D visualisation of the robot and its sensor data (pictured: a point cloud with a camera image).
  • Gazebo — simulation (pictured: a simulated indoor world; Source: automaticaddison.com).

Programming

  • Scratch / Blockly
  • G-code

  • Common programming languages:

    • Python
    • C / C++ / C#
  • Many more…

Scratch / Blockly

  • Block-based programming language developed by MIT.
  • Large library of blocks.
  • Runs on JavaScript.
  • For kids and robotics beginners.
  • Generates Python code in the background.
Unclear (slide 23)

The slide treats Scratch and Blockly as one language. Scratch was developed at the MIT Media Lab; Blockly is a separate block-programming library developed by Google. It is Blockly that generates code in text languages such as Python or JavaScript in the background; Scratch programs are not converted to Python. Both are block-based and both run in the browser.

G-code

  • Most widely used for computer numerical control (CNC) — drilling machine, lathe, mill & 3D printer.
  • Can also be used for Cartesian robots.
  • Simple, line-based command structure.
M190  S60                       ; wait for bed temp
M109  S215                      ; wait for extruder temp
G29                             ; mesh bed leveling
G1    X10 Y-3.0 Z0.5 F6000.0
G92   E0.0
G1    X60.0 E9.0 F1000.0        ; intro line
G1    X100.0 E12.5 F1000.0      ; intro line
G92   E0.0

G-code sample for a 3D printer, next to a picture of a Cartesian gantry (Source: CNC Kitchen). List of G-code commands: https://gcodetutor.com/cnc-machine-training/cnc-g-codes.html

Worked example — reading the slide's G-code line by line
  1. Identify the command type by its letter: G = motion and geometry, M = machine functions (heaters, fans); the other letters are parameters (X/Y/Z position in mm, E extruder/filament axis, F feed rate in mm/min, S a set value).
  2. M190 S60, M109 S215: heat the bed to 60\ ^\circ\text{C} and the nozzle to 215\ ^\circ\text{C}, and wait until each is reached.
  3. G29: probe the bed surface (mesh levelling).
  4. G1 X10 Y-3.0 Z0.5 F6000.0: straight-line move to (10, -3, 0.5)\ \text{mm} at 6000\ \text{mm/min} = 100\ \text{mm/s}.
  5. G92 E0.0: declare the current filament position as zero (no motion).
  6. G1 X60.0 E9.0 F1000.0: move to x = 60\ \text{mm} while feeding filament up to E = 9\ \text{mm}, at 1000\ \text{mm/min}, printing the first "intro line" that primes the nozzle. The next line continues to x = 100, feeding 12.5 - 9 = 3.5\ \text{mm} more filament.

Why it suits Cartesian robots: every motion is "go to these x, y, z coordinates in a straight line", which a gantry with one linear axis per coordinate executes directly; no inverse kinematics is needed.

Python (recommended)

  • High-level programming language.
  • It emphasizes code readability and offers a wide range of standard libraries.
  • As opposed to C-based languages, variable types do not need to be defined, but Python is "slower" when processing large data.
  • "Programming language of engineers."
  • 521.900 Einführung in Python (Introduction to Python), at the moment German only — make some noise for English classes ☺.

Pictured: a short Python snippet driving a robot forward 300 mm and turning 90° four times in a loop.

Connection

"Variable types do not need to be defined" is Python's dynamic typing from 3 Variables (Programming Prep); "slower" comes from Python being interpreted rather than compiled to machine code, as in 1 Foundations of Programming.

C / C++ / C

  • C programming language family.
  • Widely used, best CPU-performing language (family).
  • Many OS and kernels rely on C.
  • Less "user friendly".

Pictured: a C++ function (DecodeGrayCPU) decoding Gray-code image patterns with OpenCV.

Intuition

The usual split in robotics: C/C++ where speed and timing matter (motor drivers, control loops running at kHz rates, image processing, the internals of ROS), Python where development speed matters (scripts, experiments, high-level task logic, machine learning). ROS supports both, so one robot often runs a mix of C++ and Python nodes.

Simulation environments

  • Why do we need simulation environments?
  • Digital twin → digital (condition-based) monitoring and predictive maintenance.

  • Reducing costs in development:

    • Faster prototyping
    • Less need for hardware
    • Less time for experiments
    • Easy generation of training data for machine learning
Intuition

A digital twin is a simulation model of one specific real machine that is kept in sync with it by the machine's live sensor data. Comparing the real robot's behaviour (motor currents, temperatures, vibrations) with what the twin predicts shows wear before it causes a failure. Maintenance is then done when the condition requires it (condition-based), or scheduled ahead of a predicted failure (predictive maintenance), rather than at fixed intervals or after a breakdown.

Common mistake

"It works in simulation, so it works on the robot." A simulation is only as good as its models: friction, backlash, cable forces, sensor noise, lighting and contact are always simplified. A controller or a learned policy tuned in simulation can fail on hardware (the sim-to-real gap). Simulation cuts the number of real experiments; it does not remove the final test on the real robot.

Environments:

  • CoppeliaSim
  • Game engines: Unity, Unreal. Do you know any other game engines? (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_game_engines)
  • Gazebo
  • Many more…

CoppeliaSim (formerly V-REP)

  • Commercial robot simulation platform (with free educational license).
  • Allows easy integration of common robots from a library (drag & drop).
  • Advanced robot control (code and GUI) and easy sensor integration.
  • Uses Lua code; has multiple remote APIs.
  • Embedded scripts: Python & Lua (native).
  • https://www.coppeliarobotics.com/

Pictured: a real robot arm at a test stand next to its CoppeliaSim model.

Game engines

  • Game engines were designed for developing video games.
  • But due to their versatility, they can also be used to create simulation environments with robots, to create highly realistic scenarios.
  • Highly realistic models for collision, lighting, scenery.
  • Augmented & virtual reality (AR / VR).
  • Need high-performance computers and good GPUs.

Pictured: Unity and Unreal Engine logos, and a humanoid character model in an engine editor.

Gazebo

  • Free & open-source robot simulation environment with full ROS compatibility.
  • Similar to game engines, optimized for robotics applications (easy integration of ROS messages and services).

Pictured: the Gazebo logo and a simulated indoor world (Source: Addison Sears-Collins).

Intuition

Choosing a simulator is a trade-off. Gazebo speaks ROS natively, so the same nodes that will run on the real robot can be tested unchanged against the simulated one. CoppeliaSim makes it quick to drop a known robot model into a scene and script it. Game engines give the most realistic graphics (useful for camera-based perception and training data, and for AR/VR) at the cost of heavy hardware and less robotics-specific tooling.

Order of robot control

  • We just learned that a robot can be operated in multiple ways.
  • But what happens when it receives orders from multiple sources?
  • We need to give priorities → high-level vs low-level control.
  • Safety mechanisms must have the highest priority. They are always hard-wired.
  • Direct manual operation must rule over remote or automated control.

Pictured: an emergency-stop button.

Intuition

High-level control decides what to do (task logic, path planning, remote or autonomous commands); low-level control makes it happen and keeps it safe (joint controllers, limits, drives, safety circuits). The priority order puts whatever is closest to the hardware and to the person on the spot first:

PrioritySourceWhy it wins
1Hard-wired safety (e-stop, safety circuits)works even when all software has failed
2Direct manual operation at the robotthe person there sees the situation now
3Remote operationa human, but with delayed and partial view
4Programmed / autonomous controlonly knows what its sensors and code tell it
Why must safety be hard-wired rather than programmed?

Software can crash, hang, be misconfigured, or be overridden by another command, and those are exactly the moments an emergency stop is needed. A hard-wired e-stop physically interrupts the power to the motors (or the drives' enable signal) through its own circuit, so it works even if every computer has failed. A stop implemented only in software, like the ROS example above, is useful but can never be the last line of defence.
